lead: A virtual cluster is a logical group of virtual machines that is managed as one unit even though its VMs may sit on different physical hosts. A virtual data centre goes further: it gives a tenant a private view of pooled compute, storage and network drawn from a shared physical data centre. Both exist because physical hardware boundaries are too rigid and too large for one customer. Cloud providers use them to sell a slice of a building; private clouds use them to divide one building among departments.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for what a virtual machine is, 3.3 for the hypervisor layer, and 3.6 for pooled storage and network.

sections.h3: A virtual cluster is a logical cluster

blocks.text: A physical cluster is a set of hosts joined to shared storage and a network, managed as one pool: if a host dies, cluster software restarts its virtual machines elsewhere. A virtual cluster is the same idea one level up. It is a named group of virtual machines, taken from one or more hosts, managed together under one set of policies.

The group shares four things: a name and folder, a resource pool, a virtual network segment, and policies. The usual policies are high availability, which restarts a VM on a surviving host, and automated load balancing, which moves VMs when one host runs hot.

A resource pool is a container of CPU and RAM carved out of a parent host or cluster. It has three settings. A reservation is the guaranteed minimum, in MHz or GB, that the pool always gets. A limit is the maximum it may use. Shares are relative weights used only when the parent is contended: a pool with twice the shares of its sibling gets twice the contested capacity.

Virtual clusters exist because software expects several nodes. A Hadoop test cluster, a set of Kubernetes workers or a three-tier web application each wants N machines. Ten VMs on three hosts give the application its ten nodes without ten machines, and any node can be rebuilt from a template in minutes.
Remember what is logical here. Cluster membership says nothing about where the VMs sit. All ten VMs may share one physical host, and then one hardware failure takes the whole cluster down.

sections.h3: The virtual data centre: pooled resources and tenant isolation

blocks.text: A virtual data centre (VDC) is a tenant's private logical view of a data centre. It bundles a compute pool, a storage pool, a network pool, policies, quotas and a template catalogue, separated from every other tenant's VDC. The provider still owns the building, the hosts and the switches.

Build a VDC from pieces already covered: hosts grouped into clusters for compute, datastores built from LUNs or NFS exports for storage, overlay networks or VLAN segments for networking. Add role-based access so tenant A's administrator sees only tenant A's objects.

Isolation comes in layers. The hypervisor keeps the vCPUs and memory of different VMs apart. The network overlay keeps packets apart even when two VMs share one physical NIC. Storage zoning and LUN masking keep disks apart. No single layer is enough on its own.

A tenant is often sold more vCPU than the provider owns. That is oversubscription, and it is normal, because most VMs idle. A VDC described as 20 hosts of 16 vCPU may be placed on far fewer physical cores than 320.

sections.h3: Placement, migration, oversubscription and blast radius

blocks.text: Placement is the choice of host for each VM. Two rules shape it. An affinity rule keeps VMs together, for example a web server and its cache, to cut network delay. An anti-affinity rule keeps them apart, for example the two nodes of a database pair, so one host failure cannot take both.

Migration moves a running VM to another host. Live migration pauses the VM for milliseconds by copying memory pages while it runs; the mechanics belong to Unit 4. Providers use it for hardware maintenance, for balancing load across a cluster, and for emptying hosts at night to save power.
R = Σ vCPU ÷ Σ cores    U = requested capacity ÷ total capacity × 100%
blocks.where: R is the oversubscription ratio: the sum of all vCPU counts given to VMs divided by the total physical cores they can run on. R = 1 means no oversubscription; R = 4 means four virtual cores per real core. U is utilisation as a percentage, with capacity in cores, GB or MHz.

blocks.text: Admission control is the gatekeeper. When a tenant asks for a new VDC or an extra host, the manager adds the request to what is already committed, checks the reservations and limits of every pool, and refuses if a guarantee would break. It compares against committed capacity, not against the free memory of that second.

Blast radius is the set of things one failure destroys. Anti-affinity rules and separate clusters shrink it; a virtual cluster does not. A VDC narrows the tenant's blast radius from the physical site, but shared switches, shared storage arrays and shared power still remain.

figure.caption: The tenant asks for 20 hosts of 16 vCPU and 64 GB: 320 vCPU and 1,280 GB. Admission control weighs that against the whole building, 1,200 cores and 12,800 GB, not against one host — 26.7% of the CPU and 10.0% of the RAM are in use, so the virtual data centre is accepted and the oversubscription ratio is 0.27, below 1.

spec.title: Worked example: 50 hosts of 24 cores and 256 GB, one tenant asks for 20 hosts of 16 vCPU and 64 GB
spec.aria: A physical data centre of 50 hosts at 24 cores and 256 GB gives 1,200 cores and 12,800 GB; the tenant's request of 20 hosts at 16 vCPU and 64 GB gives 320 vCPU and 1,280 GB; admission control compares them, gets 26.7% CPU and 10.0% RAM use, and accepts with oversubscription ratio 0.27.

examples.question: A physical data centre has 50 hosts. Each host has 24 cores and 256 GB of RAM. A tenant asks for a virtual data centre of 20 hosts, each with 16 vCPU and 64 GB of RAM. (a) Find the physical and the requested totals. (b) Find the percentage of physical CPU and of physical RAM the request uses. (c) Should admission control accept the request, and what is the CPU oversubscription ratio?
steps: Physical cores = 50 hosts × 24 cores per host = 1,200 cores.
Physical RAM = 50 hosts × 256 GB per host = 12,800 GB.
Requested vCPU = 20 hosts × 16 vCPU per host = 320 vCPU.
Requested RAM = 20 hosts × 64 GB per host = 1,280 GB.
Both values are well under 100%, so admission control accepts. CPU oversubscription ratio R = 320 ÷ 1,200 = 0.27, below 1, so the tenant is not oversubscribed on CPU.
examples.answer: The request fits: 320 vCPU is 26.7% of 1,200 cores and 1,280 GB is 10.0% of 12,800 GB, so the virtual data centre is admitted with no CPU oversubscription.
examples.check:
cores_per_host = 24
ram_per_host = 256
hosts = 50
req_hosts = 20
vcpu_per_host = 16
ram_per_req_host = 64
total_cores = hosts * cores_per_host
total_ram = hosts * ram_per_host
req_vcpu = req_hosts * vcpu_per_host
req_ram = req_hosts * ram_per_req_host
print(req_vcpu)
print(req_ram)
print(total_cores)
print(total_ram)
print(round(req_vcpu / total_cores * 100, 1))
print(round(req_ram / total_ram * 100, 1))

traps: A virtual cluster is a logical grouping; it does not guarantee separate physical hosts or separate failure domains.
An oversubscription ratio above 1 is normal, not an error. Reservations and limits still bind, so check them before you conclude a request fits.
A virtual data centre is not a physical building. The tenant sees a private set of pools, but the provider owns every host.
Percentages are taken against the whole data centre total, not against one host. Dividing 320 by 24 cores is a classic slip.
Admission control compares the request against committed capacity minus reservations, not against the free memory at that instant.

quiz.a: A named logical group of virtual machines, drawn from one or more hosts, managed together under one set of policies such as high availability and load balancing.

quiz.q: What are reservation, limit and shares in a resource pool?
quiz.a: A reservation is the guaranteed minimum, a limit is the maximum allowed, and shares are relative weights used only when the parent resource is contended.

quiz.q: Why does forming a virtual cluster not by itself improve fault tolerance?
quiz.a: Membership is logical. The VMs may all run on one host, so a single hardware failure still removes the whole cluster. Fault tolerance needs anti-affinity rules or hosts that are physically separate.

quiz.q: A data centre has 40 hosts with 32 cores and 512 GB each. A tenant asks for 10 hosts with 8 vCPU and 128 GB each. Find the CPU and RAM utilisation percentages.
A cluster has 100 hosts with 8 cores each. VMs totalling 1,200 vCPU are placed on it. Find the oversubscription ratio and say what it means.
quiz.a: Cores = 100 × 8 = 800. R = 1,200 ÷ 800 = 1.5. The provider has sold 1.5 virtual cores per physical core, which works only while VMs stay idle for part of the time.

quiz.q: Give one difference between a virtual cluster and a virtual data centre.
quiz.a: A virtual cluster groups VMs for one application with policies such as high availability. A virtual data centre is a tenant boundary that pools compute, storage and network with quotas and isolation, and may contain several clusters.

quiz.q: A database pair runs with an anti-affinity rule. Explain how this changes the blast radius compared with a plain virtual cluster.
quiz.a: Without the rule both nodes may land on one host, so one host failure kills both and the service stops. Anti-affinity forces the nodes onto different hosts, so a host failure takes one node and the pair survives on the other. The blast radius shrinks from the whole service to one VM, at the cost of extra hosts.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry calls the combined picture a software-defined data centre: compute, storage and network are each pooled and controlled by policy, and a tenant request is filled by software. Products such as VMware vSphere with DRS and HA, and open-source OpenStack with its Nova, Neutron and Cinder projects, implement the ideas here. Newer work applies the same thinking to Kubernetes, where namespaces and virtual cluster tools give each team a private-looking cluster on shared nodes. Useful search terms: capacity planning for oversubscription, anti-affinity policy, tenant isolation in multi-tenant data centres.
